items.title: Sessions vs self-contained tokens
items.body: Server-side sessions keep state on the server and give the client an opaque ID, so revocation is immediate. Self-contained tokens such as JWTs carry signed claims verifiable without a lookup, but cannot be revoked before expiry without a denylist.
items.question: What is the usual compromise?
items.answer: Short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus longer-lived, rotating refresh tokens tracked server-side, so revocation takes effect at the next refresh.

items.title: Trusting the JWT alg header
items.question: Your JWT library picks the verification algorithm from the alg field in the token header. What attacks does this open up?
items.answer: An attacker can set alg to none, or switch RS256 to HS256 and sign with your public key used as an HMAC secret. Pin the expected algorithm and key during verification, and also validate exp, iss, and aud. RFC 8725 collects these best practices.

source.name: RFC 8725 - JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

items.title: PKCE
items.body: PKCE binds an OAuth authorization code to the client that requested it: the client sends a hash of a random code_verifier with the authorization request and the verifier itself when redeeming the code. Current OAuth security guidance recommends it for all clients.

source.name: RFC 9700 - OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice

items.title: Slow password hashes
items.question: Why store passwords with Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt instead of SHA-256?
items.answer: General-purpose hashes are built to be fast, so GPUs can test billions of guesses per second against a leaked hash. Password hashing functions are deliberately slow, Argon2 and scrypt are also memory-hard, and each hash uses a unique salt, which makes offline cracking far more expensive.

items.title: Where a SPA keeps tokens
items.question: A single-page app stores its access token in localStorage and a security review flags it. What is the concern and the usual alternative?
items.answer: Any XSS can read localStorage and exfiltrate the token for use elsewhere. An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, though XSS can still act as the user in-page, and a backend-for-frontend keeps OAuth tokens off the browser entirely. Cookies then need CSRF protection.

items.title: Authentication vs authorization
items.body: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization decides what they may do. Many breaches are authorization bugs, such as serving /orders/123 without checking that the order belongs to the caller.
